lessonTitle: Forming Basics: Hot and Cold Working, Bending and Forging versus Casting

blocks.text: A bolt-heading machine squeezes a steel wire into a finished bolt head in a fraction of a second, ten thousand times an hour. The bolt comes out stronger than the wire it was made from, and it needs no machining. The same steel heated to bright orange would form at a fraction of the force but would come out weaker, scaled and less accurate.

blocks.markdown: **Forming** shapes metal by plastic deformation rather than by removing or melting it. Main families are **forging** (compressing between dies), **rolling** (squeezing between rolls to reduce thickness), **extrusion** (pushing through a die opening) and **sheet metal forming** such as bending. The volume of metal is conserved, so material is displaced, not removed, and little is wasted.

blocks.title: Hot and cold working
blocks.text: **Hot working** deforms metal above its recrystallisation temperature. For pure metals that temperature is typically about 0.3 to 0.5 of the absolute melting temperature, and hot working is often quoted as working above about 0.5 to 0.6 of it (typical values, which vary with alloy and strain). Above it, new strain-free grains form continuously and the metal does not harden. **Cold working** deforms below that temperature, usually at room temperature, so the metal strain hardens: strength and hardness rise and ductility falls.

rows: Low: large deformation with smaller presses
Not increased by working; grain is refined and porosity closed
Higher yield strength and hardness from strain hardening
Reduced; may need annealing between stages
Large forgings, rolled beams and plate, hot extrusion
Bolts, wire drawing, sheet products, cold-rolled strip
blocks.caption: Representative comparison.

blocks.markdown: The force needed depends on the **flow stress** $\sigma_f$ of the metal at the working temperature, which is much lower hot than cold. For a simple upsetting (compression) of a cylinder, a first estimate ignores friction and gives a force equal to the flow stress times the instantaneous contact area. Friction and die shape raise the real force.

blocks.caption: Ideal upsetting force for flow stress sigma_f and contact area A (friction ignored, so this is a lower bound).

blocks.title: Upsetting force hot and cold
blocks.prompt: A steel cylinder of diameter 80 mm is upset between flat dies. Take the flow stress as 60 MPa when hot and 400 MPa when cold. Find the ideal force in each case.

steps.text: Contact area: a circle of diameter 80 mm.
Hot: force is flow stress times area, in newtons since MPa = N/mm^2.
Cold: same area with the higher flow stress.

blocks.answer: About 302 kN when hot and 2011 kN when cold, a ratio of 6.7. Hot working therefore permits a much smaller press.

blocks.markdown: **Sheet bending.** When a sheet is bent, the inside surface shortens and the outside stretches; between them is a neutral axis whose length does not change. The length of the neutral axis through the bend is the **bend allowance**. It lies at a fraction $K$ of the thickness from the inside surface, where $K$ is typically 0.33 to 0.5 (smaller for tight bends, larger for gentle ones). The flat blank length is the sum of the straight segments plus the bend allowances.

blocks.caption: Bend allowance: bend angle theta (in radians, the angle through which the sheet turns), inside bend radius R, sheet thickness t, neutral-axis factor K.

blocks.title: Bend allowance and blank length
blocks.prompt: A sheet of thickness $t=3$ mm is bent through 90 degrees with inside radius $R=4$ mm. Take $K=0.4$. A straight segment of 40 mm joins one side of the bend and a straight segment of 25 mm the other (lengths measured to the start of the bend). Find the flat blank length.

steps.text: Convert the angle to radians: 90 degrees is $\pi/2$ = 1.5708 rad.
Neutral axis radius: R + K t = 4 + 0.4 x 3 = 5.2 mm.
Blank length: straight lengths plus bend allowance: 40 + 25 + 8.168.

blocks.answer: The flat blank is 73.2 mm long; cutting 65 mm would give a short part.

blocks.markdown: **Forging versus casting.** Forging shapes solid metal and aligns the grain flow with the part contour, closes internal porosity and gives superior strength and fatigue resistance. It needs expensive dies and is limited to shapes that can be filled and ejected from the die. Casting can make complex hollow shapes in almost any size from a cheap pattern, but cast metal contains some porosity and its grain is random, so it is usually weaker and less fatigue-resistant.

items: High strength and fatigue loading with moderate complexity and large volume: forging (crankshafts, connecting rods).
Complex hollow shapes or very large parts at low volume: casting (pump housings, machine beds).
Tolerance-critical high-volume sheet parts: cold forming.
Thick sections heated and shaped in few strokes: hot forging.

blocks.title: Cold working hardens, then cracks
blocks.text: Continued cold work uses up the ductility of a metal. If the part is to be formed further, it must be annealed (heated and cooled slowly) to restore ductility, or the metal may crack.

points: Hot working is above the recrystallisation temperature: low force, no strain hardening, rough scale; cold working gives higher strength, smooth finish and accuracy but needs much more force and loses ductility.
Bend allowance is $BA=\theta (R+Kt)$ with the angle in radians; blank length is the straight lengths plus the bend allowances.
Forging gives strong, fatigue-resistant parts for volume production; casting suits complex, large or low-volume parts.

questions.stem: Which set of properties describes a part that has been cold worked rather than hot worked?

options.text: Higher yield strength, smoother surface and tighter tolerances
Lower strength, rough surface and scale
Higher ductility and lower hardness than the original bar
Identical strength to the original bar

questions.correctOptionText: Higher yield strength, smoother surface and tighter tolerances

distractorRationale.c: Cold working reduces ductility and raises hardness by strain hardening.
distractorRationale.d: Cold working changes the strength, because the metal strain hardens.

questions.explanation: Cold working strain hardens the metal, raising strength and hardness, and the absence of oxide scale and high temperature gives better finish and accuracy. The price is higher force and lower ductility.

questions.stem: Why is the force needed to forge a steel billet much lower when it is red-hot?

options.text: The flow stress falls at high temperature and the metal recrystallises, so it does not harden
The billet becomes less dense, so there is less metal to deform
Friction between the die and the billet disappears
The die expands and makes the cavity larger

questions.correctOptionText: The flow stress falls at high temperature and the metal recrystallises, so it does not harden

distractorRationale.b: Density changes slightly but volume to be deformed is unchanged.
distractorRationale.c: Friction remains and can even be higher with scale.
distractorRationale.d: Die expansion is small and does not explain the force difference.

questions.explanation: At working temperature the flow stress of steel falls and continuous recrystallisation removes strain hardening, so a smaller press suffices. Friction and the volume of metal are not eliminated.

questions.stem: A manufacturer needs 200 000 steel connecting rods that carry cyclic loads with high fatigue strength. Which process is best justified?

options.text: Closed-die forging
Sand casting
Machining each rod from a block
3D printing in polymer

distractorRationale.b: Cast metal has random grain and porosity, so lower fatigue strength.
distractorRationale.c: Machining a block wastes material and cuts across the grain flow, giving low productivity for this volume.
distractorRationale.d: Polymer would not carry the loads.

questions.explanation: Forging aligns grain with the shape, closes porosity and gives high fatigue strength, and the die cost is spread over a large volume. For high volume and fatigue loading it is the usual choice.

questions.stem: Four large pump housings with complex internal passages are needed once. Which process fits best?

options.text: Sand casting
Closed-die forging
Cold heading
Wire drawing

distractorRationale.b: Forging dies are costly and cannot make complex internal passages in low volumes.
distractorRationale.c: Cold heading forms small parts such as bolts from wire.
distractorRationale.d: Wire drawing makes wire, not housings.

questions.explanation: Casting forms complex hollow shapes using a cheap pattern and cores, so it suits low volumes of intricate large parts. Forging would need expensive dies that could not be recovered over four parts.

questions.stem: A sheet is bent through the same angle and thickness but the inside radius is increased. What happens to the bend allowance?

options.text: It increases, because the neutral axis arc becomes longer
It decreases, because the bend is gentler
It stays the same because only the angle matters
It becomes zero for large radii

questions.correctOptionText: It increases, because the neutral axis arc becomes longer

distractorRationale.b: A larger radius makes a longer arc for the same angle.
distractorRationale.c: Radius enters the formula, so it affects the allowance.
distractorRationale.d: The allowance is always positive for a nonzero angle.

questions.explanation: The bend allowance is $\theta(R+Kt)$, so with angle and thickness fixed it grows in proportion to the radius term. A larger radius gives a longer neutral axis arc through the bend.

questions.stem: A sheet of thickness 1.5 mm is bent through 120 degrees with an inside radius of 2 mm. Take $K=0.33$. Find the bend allowance in mm.
questions.explanation: The angle is $120\pi/180=2.0944$ rad and $R+Kt=2+0.33\times1.5=2.495$ mm. The bend allowance is therefore $2.0944\times2.495=5.23$ mm.

questions.stem: A sheet of thickness 2.5 mm is bent through 90 degrees with inside radius 5 mm (take $K=0.4$). The straight segments are 50 mm and 35 mm, measured to the start of the bend. Find the flat blank length in mm.
questions.explanation: The bend allowance is $(\pi/2)(5+0.4\times2.5)=9.42$ mm. Adding the straight segments gives $50+35+9.42=94.42$ mm for the flat blank.

questions.stem: A steel cylinder of diameter 60 mm is hot upset between flat dies with a flow stress of 70 MPa. Ignoring friction, find the force in kN.
questions.explanation: The area is $\pi\times60^2/4=2827.4$ mm^2. The ideal force is $70\times2827.4=197.9$ kN. Friction would raise the actual force above this value.

questions.stem: Compare hot and cold working in terms of strength of the product, surface finish, dimensional accuracy and the force required. Give an example product for each.
markingGuide: Hot: above recrystallisation temperature, no strain hardening, low flow stress and force
Hot: rough scaled surface and poorer accuracy; example large forging or rolled beam
Cold: strain hardening gives higher strength and hardness but lower ductility
Cold: smooth finish and good accuracy but higher force; example bolt or cold-rolled strip
Notes annealing may be needed in cold working
questions.explanation: The comparison is driven by recrystallisation: hot working avoids strain hardening and so needs less force, while cold working retains it for strength and accuracy. Giving a suitable example for each shows the trade-off in use.

questions.stem: A wheel hub for a rail vehicle is needed in batches of 20 000 with high fatigue loading, while a large valve body with internal passages is needed three times. Select forging or casting for each and justify the choice.
markingGuide: Hub: forging, because of grain flow, strength and fatigue resistance
Hub: high volume justifies the die cost
Valve body: casting, because complex internal passages and large size can be made with cores and cheap patterns
Valve body: low volume does not justify forging dies
Mentions a trade-off or limitation of the other process, such as porosity in castings or die cost in forging
questions.explanation: The selection depends on strength requirements, geometry and volume. Forging is justified by fatigue strength at high volume; casting by complexity and low volume.
